subtopic: MEASURE TO AMPLIFY FREIGHT RATES LEGISLATION, TO REMOVE CERTAIN STATUTORY REDUCTIONS, AND OTHER MATTERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the introduction of this bill because at least it recognizes a principle which we on this side have been advocating for so long, namely, that some assistance should be given immediately to shippers and plants in the Atlantic provinces to enable them to compete in the Canadian market.
I am glad the minister has finally brought this bill into the house. As he has indicated, it is only an interim measure but I feel it will bring some degree of relief to those affected and it does recognize the principle we have been advocating that subsidies should be paid to all modes of transportation, not just to the railways. Our trucking industry has suffered for years as a result of inequitable competition, and I know this bill will be welcomed with some degree of relief.
Since I welcome the legislation I do not wish to impede its passage, but there are three or four questions I should like to put to the minister for clarification. First, why should it be necessary to bring in a completely new act under a new title? Those who have studied the report of the Atlantic premiers will have noted that while the premiers wanted many changes they worked on the assumption that those changes would be made to the existing Maritime Freight Rates Act. I do not think this was merely because the old name was familiar to them; there may be a good basis for the position they took. The Maritime Freight Rates Act finally, by statute, recognized not only the constitutional obligations assumed at the time of confederation but also the many commitments which have been made over the years to the Atlantic provinces-that they were entitled to certain subsidies to enable them to compete in the Canadian market, and so on. I am not a legal authority and maybe this point is not well taken, but it seems to me there is a feeling that the bringing in of a completely new act, one which does not include these commitments in the preamble, will mean these commitments may be lost in the shuffle. Yet they are the basis of the special claim for assistance advanced by the maritimes. Why could not the old act have been reopened and revised to include the word "Atlantic" if that 
is considered desirable? Possibly the minister could explain this to us later.
The second point has already been mentioned by the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants (Mr. McCleave). Here again I should like to refer to the report of the four premiers. It seems to me that if we are really interested in assisting the Atlantic region we should certainly listen to the presentations and requests of those directly involved. This was always the position taken by the former Minister of Transport. Every time we questioned him as to what was being done to assist maritime transportation he told us he was awaiting the premiers' report. Now we have that report. It confirms what we heard in almost every brief submitted to us during the trip through the Atlantic provinces, first, that subsidies should be paid not to the truckers or the carriers but to the shippers. The fear was many times expressed that if the subsidies were not paid to the shippers they would not receive the full benefit.
In the second place the premiers felt that the subsidies should be administered by an agency they proposed to set up in the Atlantic provinces. As reason for this, they said the subsidy should be allocated on a selective basis; it should be used to assist industry and should be capable of adjustment as need for assistance was required. They felt this could best be arranged by an agency composed of people from the Atlantic region with an intimate knowledge of local conditions. I would therefore ask the minister to tell us why the government has decided that the subsidy should be administered by the Governor in Council rather than by a separate agency as proposed.
[DOT] (12:20 p.m.)
The third point I want to raise is in connection with the premiers' report. Running through the report one will find the distinct theme that change should not be made by the dominion government just for the sake of change or to save money. In more than one place in the report it is stated that if the government of Canada alters the Maritime Freight Rates Act it must accept responsibility for making sure that any changes that are made are for the purpose of assisting the region, not just to save money.
At page 14 of the Atlantic premiers' report appears this statement:
In fact, the modification of the Maritime Freight Rates Act proposed in this report is made by the four governments on the clear understanding that
June 17, 1969	COMMONS
the acceptance of such modification by the federal government is equally an acceptance by that government of the responsibility to ensure that the revised act substantially improves the marketing position of regional industry both now and in the long term.
This is something that the premiers emphasized and that I also would like to emphasize.
Fourth and last, I do not see any specified amount of funds provided by the bill to pay subsidies. I should like to know whether there is any limitation on the amount. Subclause 2 of clause 3 of the bill makes reference to a ceiling on assistance payable of 30 per cent of the charges for movement of goods by any individual carrier, but I should like to know whether the total amount of funds available by way of subsidy is limited. Perhaps the minister would clarify that point later.
Briefly, those are the points I wanted to make. I welcome this temporary measure and I hope it will be an interim one. I ask the minister to give full consideration to the committee's report. Many of the suggestions should and must be adopted right away if we are to develop a viable Atlantic transportation act. We suggest that subsidies are very important to the maritimes, and we suggest they be granted on a selective basis and administered in such a way as to encourage industries to develop into viable enterprises. I hope the minister will consider these remarks as well as the report of the committee, and that in the near future we can expect an over-all transportation policy for the maritimes.

subtopic: MEASURE TO AMPLIFY FREIGHT RATES LEGISLATION, TO REMOVE CERTAIN STATUTORY REDUCTIONS, AND OTHER MATTERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the normal reaction of hon. members would be that we are in a rather strange position procedurally at the moment in being asked to deal with the second reading of this bill on the eve of receiving and discussing a comprehensive report made by a parliament standing committee which it has been indicated will be placed before the house later today. One's normal reaction is that this is a pretty bad case of putting the cart before the horse. However, inasmuch as there seems to be some indication of agreement to this course of action on the part of members of the transport committee, who recently made a rather extensive tour of the Atlantic region, perhaps other hon. members will go along with this proposal on the understanding given them by the minister that this bill represents an interim and perhaps temporary measure.
Atlantic Regional Freight Assistance Act
There are one or two aspects of the bill about which I am concerned, particularly with reference to the extension of subsidies to truckers. I hope the minister and the government are not going to go overboard in this respect. I have sensed a disposition on the part of truckers in the various representations they have made to the members of this house over quite a period of years to feel that they have some sort of divine right to equality of position with the railways in regard to matters such as this and in relation to transportation generally. My concern is that if this matter is not watched very carefully we are going to find ourselves, in effect, in the position of paying a double subsidy. In other words, we are going to be subsidizing truckers, even though the result of their operations will be to reduce the volume of traffic provided to the railways. Therefore we will find ourselves in the position of subsidizing two uneconomic operations.
I think this discussion stems from the debate in the house at the time the National Transportation Act was under consideration. In my view that act was a rather peculiar one. It set a precedent that I am not sure is at all desirable in that when it was introduced it contained a kind of preamble. Actually it was not a preamble but a clause of the bill which in effect set forth a particular philosophy of approach to transportation matters.
I am concerned that in the follow-through from the passage of that act there is going to be a slavish adherence to the principle of supporting the virtues of competition for competition's sake, rather than the recognition that in a matter as basic to the economy as transportation there are situations where the concept of complementing one form of transportation with another is really a more economically sensible approach. In my view the practical effect of slavishly following the concept of the virtues of competition is that we in this country will indulge in a lot of wasteful and uneconomical capital expenditure. I think we have an historic reason to be concerned about this happening. The whole history of the boom of railway construction, competitive railway lines and the resulting chaos that eventually caused parliament to place severe restrictions on the operation of the railways and the construction of ne v railway lines should, I think, be kept in mind by the parliamentarians of this generation. It has been argued that the wasteful expenditure of capital funds at that time seriously endangered the proper growth and development of Canada as a nation.
10234	COMMONS
Atlantic Regional Freight Assistance Act
On the other hand, coming back again to the relationship between the truckers and the railway companies, I think we should recall that by its acts at that period of our history parliament emphasized the original understanding of the Fathers of Confederation, namely, that in a country such as ours the railways were, and in my view still are, basic to our liability as a nation. I do not think the interests of any particular group of truck lines should be allowed to supersede our understanding of that basic concept as far as the movement of bulk goods in this country is concerned.
[DOT] (12:30 p.m.)
I would not want it to be said that I am arguing that there is no place for proper support of the trucking industry in the provision of transportation services to the producers and shippers of this country. At the same time I remind the house that one of the things that must go with that is the expenditure of major funds in the construction of highways. This burden will in large part fall on the taxpayers of Canada at the provincial level, although some of the requisite funds for this region will be provided by the government of Canada through federally raised taxes. These are some of the considerations that came to my mind as I listened to the minister introducing this interim measure to assist transportation in the Atlantic region.

Mr. Speaker, may I begin by saying I regret that the minister has found it necessary to bring in a temporary measure in order to deal with the urgent needs and problems of maritime transportation. I was a member of the committee and toured the maritimes earlier this year. We heard many briefs and saw much evidence to substantiate the fact that transportation is a problem of major dimensions in the maritimes. The very fact that for many years the Maritime Freight Rates Act has been on our statute books indicates that this problem is of long standing. I am therefore disappointed that the newly appointed minister from that region has brought in a temporary measure. We have had problems with transportation in the maritimes almost since confederation. Why did he, therefore, introduce temporary legislation? Why did he not introduce substantially different and new legislation? After all, we want to solve the transportation difficulties in the maritimes.
This bill, which in my opinion will not be as beneficial as the Maritime Freight Rates Act was, will assist only the trucking industry in the maritimes. Its provisions will make available to truckers hauling goods out of the region assistance that was formerly available under the Maritime Freight Rates Act. Smaller operators carrying on trucking operations within the maritimes will not be helped. As I read the bill it seems that there is to be no assistance to truckers moving goods to the area.
Why should the Governor in Council be involved in regulations governing truckers? Trucking concerns operating within the region will have to come to the Governor in Council for authority to do certain things. Why should a trucker or his agent have to lobby the minister in order to obtain a
June 17, 1969	COMMONS
licence? Surely the provisions of clause 3 are not fair. It is not fair for people to have to beg the Governor in Council for permission to do anything. Why should anyone have to go on bended knee and ask for assistance?

speechtext: What difference does that make, Mr. Speaker? We now have another committee, another board. Any assistance made available to the trucking industry may not be passed on to shippers. In other words, shippers may not benefit. It is well known that the railways set the basic freight rates and that truckers tag along. If truckers are to be given a subsidy it may mean that they will make greater profits and not pass on to shippers the benefits of any assistance. Frankly, I doubt very much that the trucking industry will pass on to its customers the benefit of any assistance. I do not think this legislation will have much effect on truckers hauling goods out of the maritime region. I think this is a disappointing piece of legislation which does not go far enough in meeting the very serious transportation problems the maritime region has experienced almost since confederation. It will do little to improve those economic factors that tie our country together.

In my hand I have a news release dated June 13, 1969. It says in part:
The new bill incorporates the substances of Bill C-182 introduced on March 19. 1969, wider which it was proposed to extend for one year the existing freeze on non-competitive carload rail freight rates on Atlantic region shipments, but it provides that the freeze can be terminated before the end of the year by the Governor in Council.
What kind of security are we giving the transportation industry of the maritime region? The freeze is to be extended for one year. Yet, as the news release says, the freeze can be terminated at any time before the end 29180-647J
Atlantic Regional Freight Assistance Act of this year-before December 31, 1969. How can the government act with such permanency on some matters and yet take such temporary action with regard to some of the more important economic factors that bind us together? These economic factors must be made cohesive.
[DOT] (12:40 p.m.)
This bill does not go far enough. It does not ensure that the shipper will receive the benefits. It does not give any real benefit to the trucking industry except to the large trucking firms, and it gives all power to the committee that the minister is establishing.
I have one suggestion to make to the minister. I know it will be difficult for him to follow me without having a copy of the National Transportation Act in front of him. The Maritime Freight Rates Act has been in existence for many years, but even the National Transportation Act makes special provision for the movement of grain for export over railroads leading to eastern ports. This is the eastern grain policy. It was promoted to provide for the continued development of harbours such as Halifax and Saint John. I believe it would also be possible to build another large port on Bay d'Espoir.
Surely the concept of the development and continuance of the harbours in the Atlantic region should be incorporated into a new Maritime Freight Rates Act. When the standing committee visited the maritimes we received many briefs about containerization which will modernize the whole transportation industry. Surely such transportation legislation should give consideration to inbound freight arriving at Halifax for transportation into the interior of the country.
The other point I wish to raise with the minister concerns the right of appeal by a carrier within a region. I discussed this matter with knowledgeable men serving on the Atlantic Transportation Commission. Section 16(3) of the National Transportation Act reads:
In conducting an investigation under this section, the Commission shall have regard to all considerations that appear to it to be relevant, including, without limiting the generality of the foregoing,
(a) whether the tolls or conditions specified for the carriage of traffic under the rate so established are such as to create
(i) an unfair disadvantage beyond any disadvantage that may be deemed to be inherent in the location or volume of the traffic, the scale of operation connected therewith, or the type of traffic or service involved-
10236	COMMONS
Atlantic Regional Freight Assistance Act
In other words, if the disadvantage is because of location or smallness of volume of traffic there is no appeal to the new C.T.C.
I asked the Atlantic transportation people about this section. I asked whether they felt they had ample room to appeal any case under it to the C.T C. They immediately replied no because this provision prohibits an appeal on the ground of location or smallness of traffic. I suggested removing the word "beyond" from the subsection and they said that would improve the act 100 per cent and would give them an opportunity to appeal any unfair rate that may be imposed upon them, whether it be because of their location or because of the small amount of traffic. This would not be a subsidy. This would not be a grant of money. It would just give them an equal opportunity with persons in other regions to appeal to the Canadian Transport Commission.
The minister has told us that a more permanent piece of legislation with respect to the Maritime Freight Rates Act will be coming before the house in the fall. I repeat that I recommend to him that he give consideration to removing the word "beyond" from section 16(3) of the National Transportation Act. There is no question in my mind that this subsection does not apply to Ontario central Canada, although it might apply to some vast regions of the west. But as it is now worded it certainly does apply to the Atlantic region.
If the minister is going to make a subsidy available to the trucking industry he should do so in such a way that the benefit will be passed on to the shipper. Second, he should give consideration in more permanent legislation to provisions governing outgoing export traffic similar to those provisions covering the eastern export of grain. Containerization can add to the permanency of some of the great all-winter ports that we have on the east coast. My third suggestion is that he delete the word "beyond" from section 16(3) of the National Transportation Act.

I also suggest, if the freeze on non-competitive rates is to continue, that it should not continue just until the end of the year. Let us give some permanency to it if it is justified because of there being no corridor road through the state of Maine or because of a number of other reasons such as there being no causeway to Prince Edward Island. A number of reasons could be brought forward for the freeze remaining, but let us not have

it at the prerogative of the Governor in Council so that it may be discontinued at the end of a six month period. speakeroldname: Hon. Donald C. Jamieson (Minister of Transport):
subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER AS TO ROLE OF FEDERAL AUTHORITY-TIRE FAILURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last week I advised the house that I would be making a statement on road and motor vehicle traffic safety. As hon. members are aware, responsibility for the federal government's role and leadership in this field has been assigned to the Department of Transport. When the department had identified all aspects of this problem in which the federal government had concern or responsibility the departments responsible for motor vehicle administration and highway safety of each of the ten provincial governments were individually and collectively consulted so that the department could define a program by which the federal government might make the greatest possible contribution. These preliminary discussions were successfully concluded when my predecessor met in Quebec City on January 14 of this year with the ten provincial ministers responsible for motor vehicle administration.
As the house was told following the conference, the provincial ministers welcomed the suggestion of an expanded role by the federal government in certain fields related to traffic safety and specifically in the field of traffic safety research, in facilitating international co-operation in the field of safety research and in developing safety standards for motor vehicles and parts at the point of manufacture.
The federal and provincial ministers also agreed on further periodic consultations to ensure the closest co-ordination of programs and the most profitable exchange of views. As a result of the proposed future ministerial meetings, one of which will be held in September of this year, the appointment of the Public Advisory Board previously envisaged has been deferred. For the present it is believed that the periodic discussions between the federal and provincial ministers and our officials will provide the required source of information for the guidance of our program on motor vehicles and highway safety.
On January 1, 1969, the Road and Motor Vehicle Traffic Safety Office was officially established in the Department of Transport with the appointment of a director. The program of this office will be related to: (1) safety standards for new motor vehicles and parts at the point of manufacture in or importation into Canada; (2) co-ordination of all federal
Federal Authority on Tire Safety government activities related to road safety; (3) correlation of road safety research in Canada; (4) international liaison in matters related to road and motor vehicle traffic safety; and (5) planning and support of research programs.
Legislation to establish mandatory safety standards for new motor vehicles and components, including tires, at the point of manufacture in or importation into Canada is now being actively considered. Twenty-nine motor vehicle safety standards have been prepared and issued by the Canadian Government Specifications Board, while additional standards are under study. These standards could be promulgated as soon as suitable legislation has been adopted. Consideration is also being given to means for ensuring compliance with standards. Pending the adoption of federal legislation, Canadian motor vehicle manufacturers and importers have given the government assurances that new motor vehicles and components, including tires, sold in Canada will comply with the existing federal safety standards. The Canadian manufacturers and importers have also agreed to notify the Department of Transport and purchasers of any defect coming to their attention bearing on the safety of vehicles manufactured by them.
The Road and Motor Vehicle Traffic Safety Office has been working with other federal departments on road problems related to safety, such as traffic control devices. The office is working with various national organizations such as the Canadian Good Roads Association to correlate the numerous road research activities throughout Canada.
[DOT] (2:10 p.m.)
The office is actively participating in the road research service and working party on automobile safety of the International Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development. It is also monitoring the activities of the working party on road safety of the Economic Commission for Europe which is attempting to prepare international motor vehicle safety standards. Contacts have been established with the ministries in France, Great Britain and the United States responsible for traffic safety.
As staff is recruited for the new office during the current fiscal year, their efforts will be directed toward the compilation of an inventory of current road safety research in Canada, an assessment of the needs for an
June 17, 1969

Federal Authority on Tire Safety improved documentation centre, the identification of all safety-oriented activities and their inter-relationships, and the drafting of a modest research program which may effectively contribute to the reduction of crashes, fatalities, injuries and property damage on Canadian roads.
The principal features of the government's initiative in the field of road and motor vehicle traffic safety are co-ordination of activities with the provinces to avoid unnecessary duplication of effort and co-operation with industry, safety organizations and other interested groups. This is typified by the agreement worked out with the provincial ministers to limit federal safety standards to new motor vehicles and components, leaving the control of safety for vehicles in use on the highway systems with the provinces who have the necessary legislation and administrative machinery to regulate this aspect of the problem.
I might add a word with regard to the recent comments and questions which I have been asked on tire failures. The information recently released on the results of tests performed on tires by the national highway safety bureau of the U.S. Department of Transportation was based on a sample comprising 176 tires from 15 different United States manufacturers. The test involved only replacement tires. No testing of original equipment tires- which account for one third of all tires produced-is being done by the United States bureau. Of the 176 tires tested, 33 or 18 per cent failed one or more of the separate laboratory tests for endurance, high speed operation, penetration strength, bead unseating, dimensions and labelling. Due to the difficulty in interpreting the results from such a limited sample, the United States national highway safety bureau began in January an additional testing program on 1,900 tires. No results are as yet available from these tests. The Department of Transport will be studying the results of the new United States testing program and will be particularly interested in the relationship between the results of these empirical laboratory tests and results from actual use on the road.
No results are available from similar tests on Canadian tires to indicate non-compliance with Canadian standards. As previously announced, the government is now considering legislation requiring mandatory safety standards for new motor vehicles and components, including tires. Safety standards for used vehicles, including replacement tires,


are a provincial responsibility. Most provinces now specify in their motor vehicle or highway traffic acts that replacement tires shall conform to a standard similar to that enforced by the United States bureau. When federal legislation is enacted, it may be possible to arrange a tire standard program jointly with the provinces to ensure compliance in both original equipment and replacement tires.

I am very glad to hear that the minister is going to take an active part in safety research and the standardization of safety equipment in the manufacture of motor vehicles, and particularly in the co-ordination between the activities of the federal government, such as they may be, and those of the provincial governments.

The Department of Public Works would be involved because of its connection with roads and highways. Trade and Industry will certainly be affected because of the connection with manufacturing and safety standards. The Department of Transport, into whose hands the whole matter seems to have been dumped, is of course concerned. The National Research Council will have a role to play and, from the minister's remarks, it appears that even the Department of Consumer Affairs may be involved. suggest the minister consider appointing a special committee to look into the matter and to make recommendations. speechtext:
The announcement made by the Minister of Transport has to do with a very serious problem, one which affects Canadians everywhere. For some years we have been killing on our highways rather more than 100 persons each week, injuring over 3,000 every week and causing economic losses running into many millions of dollars.
There are three main causes of accidents: one, the driver; two, the vehicle, and three, the highway. In 1967 several hon. members of this house, who had private members bills down on the order paper calling for action with regard to various aspects of traffic safety, undertook to remove their bills from the list when the government agreed to send their subject matter to the committee on Justice and Legal Affairs for study. After careful consideration some major recommendations were made by the committee, one of which was put into effect last week by the enactment of the drinking-driving law.
The minister's announcement today, though it leaves something to be desired, does represent a step forward with regard to the co-ordination of federal, provincial and industrial action to control the number of accidents and improve car safety ingredients, as well as the highway system itself. I wish to express some disappointment over the fact that the minister failed to announce the appointment of the public safety board to which reference was made by his predecessor. Only a week ago the Canadian Automobile Association, which has a million members, urged the government to appoint such a board, whose purpose would be to work for greater safety on our highways. I urge the
Federal Authority on Tire Safety minister to consider making appointments to this board soon.
As a measure of the gravity of this subject, may I say that while we have been speaking on this matter at least one Canadian has been killed on our highways, some 30 have been injured, and the toll in dollars has amounted to over $100,000.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER AS TO ROLE OF FEDERAL AUTHORITY-TIRE FAILURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we quite agree that road safety should be watched closely in the country.
In fact, when the minister insists on the fact that standards of security will have to be applied more and more during the construction of the vehicles themselves, we agree all the way, but we feel that it is not the main factor in all the accidents that happen.
It may be that the best car will carry more guarantees than it really offers against defects capable of causing serious accidents. Of course, this can be remedied, but I believe that this is only a minute part of the problem and that road security rests on the education and training of the drivers. Indeed, these two factors represent the biggest cause of the accidents which we all deplore and which are now almost innumerable. It all depends, in the majority of cases, on the training of the driver, and on his sense of responsibility towards himself and other drivers.
Drivers' incompetence and carelessness, in special circumstances sometimes, should be looked into. The training of those who are granted a driver's permit should be checked. That is a provincial matter, of course, but the federal government can help the provinces to improve the education of all drivers of motor vehicles.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-FAILURE TO RELIEVE ALLEGED CRITICAL CASH POSITION OF WESTERN CANADIAN FARMERS
speechtext:
That this house condemns the government for its failure to take steps to relieve the critical cash position of farmers in western Canada.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the motion I have moved is very clear and concise. It simply states that this house condemns the government for its failure to relieve the critical cash position of farmers in western Canada. Anyone who is familiar with the prairie provinces knows that the plight of western farmers is serious.
Alleged Failure to Aid Western Farmers
The first point I would like to make is that the plight of the grain economy in western Canada is not due to any failure on the part of the farmers themselves. In the past 20 years they have trebled the production per farm worker. No other industry in Canada can match this tremendous achievement. The farmer today is the victim of his own ingenuity, hard work and technological innovation. No one should blame the farmers for producing wheat which the government unfortunately is not able to sell; nor should the farmers be penalized because of this.
Last summer the farmers of western Canada were assured by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) that we would be able to export an average of 430 million bushels a year for the next three years. In his speech in the city of Winnipeg on June 2, 1968, the Prime Minister told the people of western Canada that it was the plan of his government to sell in the export market 1,300 million bushels of wheat over the next three years. Therefore the farmers have done their part; they have certainly produced an abundance of wheat.
The problem which faces the western economy is one for which the federal government must accept full responsibility. Its failure to meet that responsibility merits the motion of condemnation I am now moving. The first thing which I think the house must become fully aware of is the fact that the western farmer is facing a cash income crisis. During the past two years there has been a steady decline both in wheat sales and wheat prices. Exports for the first eight months of the present crop year are down 19 per cent from the ten-year average. Our carryover of wheat is estimated to be 15 per cent above the 1967-68 crop year. It is estimated that at the end of this crop year we will have some 944 million bushels of wheat on hand. This means that if we have an average crop this year we will have before Christmas in Canada approximately 1,500 million bushels of wheat carryover-an all-time high.
Not only have sales of wheat been declining but the price the farmer receives has been declining. The final realized wheat price for the 1967-68 crop year was down 17.8 cents per bushel; for barley the final received price was down 9.4 cents per bushel, and oats were down 1-| cents per bushel compared with the previous crop year. At the same time, the Wheat Board is selling wheat below the I.G.A. floor price of $1,954 a bushel; therefore this figure has become virtually meaningless in so far as the farmer is concerned.
10250	COMMONS
Alleged Failure to Aid Western Farmers
[DOT] (3:10 p.m.)
Another factor contributing to declining farm cash income has been the substantial reduction in delivery quotas which the farmer is able to dispose of at the country elevator. Wheat marketings to April 23 were 236.7 million bushels compared with 320 million bushels at the same time last year. This represents a decline of 26 per cent. As of June 10 of last year, in the province of Saskatchewan there were no delivery points on a three-bushel quota or less. In the present crop year, 55 per cent of the delivery points are on a three-bushel quota or less. Last year, 38 per cent of all delivery points were on six bushels or more, whereas in the present crop year no delivery points are on a six-bushel quota.
Last Friday the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin), who has the Canadian Wheat Board under his jurisdiction, is reported in Hansard at page 10096 as having said:
There are at present 4 on unit quota, 19 stations on a one-bushel quota, 204 on two bushels, 579 on three bushels, 684 on lour bushels, and 347 on live bushels. I am assured by the chief commissioner that his hopes are still very high that all stations will be on a five-bushel quota by the end of the crop year.
His hopes may be high, but I submit there is very little likelihood of there being a five-bushel quota for all stations in western Canada. The government may announce a five-bushel quota, but will there be space into which the farmer can deliver a five-bushel quota? That is the important question which I hope the government will answer today.
The Canadian Federation of Agriculture in the brief which they presented to the government on May 28, 1969, pointed out that in this year there will be a reduction in grain income for the western farmers of $430 million, of which $140 million will represent a reduction in deliveries of grain. There will be a further decline of $290 million in the Wheat Board's spring payments which this year will amount to less than $70 million compared with $360 million in the last crop year.
I submit that a decline of $430 million in the cash income of the grain growers of western Canada is a staggering blow to the western economy. No other section of our economy is experiencing such a drastic reduction in its income. Furthermore, I wish to point out that the farmers' situation is aggravated by the increased costs of production. Much of their grain from last year was damp and farmers had the additional expense of drying

DEBATES	June 17, 1969
it. Also, they received lower grades for that grain. Much of the grain had to be stored which involved additional carrying charges. Because of the policies and lack of policies of this government the farmers are paying the highest interest rates in the history of this country. They are paying higher prices for their machinery, equipment, lumber, hardware and the other items which they need in order to continue their farming operation.
It is not only the farmers who are feeling the effects of the catastrophic drop in farm cash income. The entire prairie economy is feeling the effects. Retail sales in Saskatchewan for the first four months of 1969 were down 11 per cent compared with 1968, and last year they were down 4.5 per cent compared with 1967. Machinery sales in Saskatchewan are down some 26.2 per cent and in Manitoba they are down 18.4 per cent. Automobile sales are down 8J per cent. The fact is that the western economy is in deep trouble, and it is not in this situation because it has failed to produce. It is in these dire straits because the government has failed to formulate policies to stabilize prices and to market the grain crops which the farmers have produced in such abundance.
I want to make two broad proposals. First, I want to talk about the need for an immediate short-term policy to improve the cash position of the prairie farmers. The Standing Committee on Agriculture recognized this need when it asked the government to alleviate the critical cash position of farmers in the predominantly grain growing areas of western Canada. That committee, after touring the west, recognized the need for a massive infusion of cash into the pockets of the farmers of western Canada if the western economy is to be saved.
There are a number of proposals as to how the government can provide some immediate cash income. For instance, the New Democratic party has proposed that the government might pay a 20 cents per bushel deficiency payment on all grain delivered to the Canadian Wheat Board in the crop year 196768 up to a maximum of 5,000 bushels. The advantages of this proposal are, first, that the records are readily available and the money could be sent out speedily and, second, that it would be pinpointed directly to the farmers who make their main livelihood from growing grain. The Federation of Agriculture in its brief to the government on May 28 last proposed an acreage payment of $2 an acre up to a maximum of 1,000 acres. The government can use either of these techniques, a
June 17, 1969

combination of them, or any other method they prefer, but the immediate need is to get cash into the pockets of the prairie farmers to enable them to finance their summer fallowing and harvesting operations and to provide a stimulant to the prairie economy.
In addition to this proposal the Canadian Federation of Agriculture in their brief made to the government what I think is a very reasonable proposal for a four-year commitment of $160 minion for 1970, declining by $40 mfilion a year thereafter, this money to be used for direct income assistance, partly for acreage reduction and partly for livestock incentive programs or any other useful agricultural policies designed to benefit the western farmer. If the present grain situation calls for a greater diversification of western agriculture, then surely the government must give the lead and supply the necessary finances to enable the farmers to make that transition.
I say to the government that the time for action is long overdue. For six months now the government has stalled and procrastinated. Day after day we have asked questions of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson), and the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce as to what they are going to do about the serious situation on the prairies. It is not a new situation; it has been growing worse for over two years now. What sort of replies have we had? We have been told that the matter is under review and that the whole question is being given consideration. We were told that the government was waiting for the report of the committee on agriculture. We were told that they were waiting until they heard from the National Farmers Union and waiting until they could meet the provincial Ministers of Agriculture and the deputy ministers. Now they have run out of excuses and recently they have merely been saying that the matter is under active consideration.

I also want to say something about the need for a long-term policy to provide markets for wheat and other cereal grains at stabilized price levels. In the short time available to me I cannot outline in detail the many points which ought to be included in a long-

Alleged Failure to Aid Western Farmers term program. I should like to deal with the need for a transport controller to provide more equitable deliveries for farmers. speakeroldname: Hon. Jean-Luc Pepin (Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce

speechtext:
No, to the first question; yes, to the second.
Well, that is simple enough, Mr. Speaker. With the government embarking on a price war in wheat and the Canadian Wheat Board selling wheat below $1,954 a bushel, the entire cost is being placed on the backs of the farmers, and I submit that the least the government could do would be to acknowledge that those who produce our wheat should at least be getting the floor price. If, because of government policy, we have to sell wheat below the floor price the difference should be made up from the national treasury by all the people of Canada.
The second point I wish to stress is the need for a two-price system. The Canadian wheat producer is the only grower in the world whose domestic price is set by world markets. Other countries provide farmers with a price for their domestic sales which is in keeping with general price levels. This is the least the government could do and, in fact, the Standing Committee on Agriculture has recommended such a step in its report.
When I make these suggestions about a guaranteed price for wheat and a two-price system which would set the domestic price at a figure bearing a fair relationship to the farmers' cost of production I am not suggesting anything to which the liberal party is not committed. I remind the house that in March, 1963, when the Liberal party was in opposition, in the election campaign of that year the 
DEBATES	June 17, 1969
Right Hon. L. B. Pearson, speaking in the City of Saskatoon, pledged that if he and his friends were elected to office they would guarantee the farmers of western Canada $2 a bushel for their wheat and would institute a two-price system. This was six years ago. When are hon. members opposite going to keep their promise? When are they going to keep faith with the farmers of western Canada? What are the Liberal representatives in the cabinet doing to see that the Liberal party honours a commitment which its leader at the time made to the people of western Canada?
The third thing I wish to suggest in relation to a long-term program is that we need an aggressive and imaginative sales campaign to sell wheat and other stable grains. There is much talk about a lack of food on the market. As a matter of fact there is no surplus of food in the world. The F.A.O. has made it clear that the per capita production of food in the world is less this year than it was in 1939. There are parts of the world in which food supplies have grown faster than population. But throughout the major part of the world the population has grown faster than the food supply. The lack is not one of demand for food; it is the lack of effective demand for food. The problem is that those who need food both in other lands and in our own land do not have the means to pay for it.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
I wonder whether the government is really applying itself to the task of seeing whether or not we can meet some of the demand for food. Even in our own country I am not convinced we are meeting the full demand for food. The economic Council of Canada speaks of some five million people living below the poverty line, of nearly eight million living below the line of deprivation. Does anyone suggest they are getting all the food they need? I notice that the Canada Dairy Commission estimate that in 1969-70 they will have on hand 200 million pounds of powdered milk, five-sixths of which will still belong to the Dairy Commission.
In the United States and other lands hot school lunches are being supplied to school children as well as a pint of milk per day for each child. The United States is using the food stamp plan by which old age pensioners, veterans, widows and their children and other needy people are given books of food stamps at nominal cost with which they can buy food, the stamps being redeemed by the government at current prices. Has the government really investigated whether or not
June 17, 1969	COMMONS
the people of Canada are consuming all the food they are now capable of using.
I am wondering whether the government has looked into the possibility of selling food, particularly wheat and cereal grains, to other parts of the world? For years the government has been coasting on the large wheat orders received from Mainland China and the Soviet Union. If we are going to sell wheat we must develop long-term, bilateral trade agreements.
I am convinced there is a steady market for wheat in countries like the Soviet Union, where it is cheaper to get their Siberian requirements from western Canada than it is to bring them all the way from the Ukraine. There are possibilities for a permanent market in Mainland China; the problem is how the Chinese can pay us. They can only pay if we work out some type of two-way trade. It may be necessary in some instances to accept partial payment in soft currencies, as the United States has been doing, and it may also be necessary to enter into long-term credit arrangements.
Canada is committed to increasing its foreign aid to one per cent of its gross national product. We are only doing about half of what we have committed ourselves to do. It seems to me that a very large part of the increase that we ought to undertake in our foreign aid commitments should be in the form of food to countries that cannot afford to pay for it. I believe we could step up our contributions of foreign aid through the World Food Bank so that much of what we now call our glut of food could be made available to the hungry people of the world.
It is all very well for the Prime Minister to say that it is not his job to sell wheat, but I point out that the Wheat Board Act does place this responsibility squarely on his shoulders and on the shoulders of his ministers, particularly the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin). At the present time the western farmer is paying for both the government's and the minister's incompetence. The time has come for the government to demonstrate it has the initiative and imagination to cope with the difficult problem of selling wheat in a world where hungry nations lack Canadian dollars to purchase that wheat.
The fact is that in this regard we have not even held our own. In the period 1948 to 1952 we had 21.3 per cent of the world's grain market. In 1967-68 our share had declined to only 11.6 per cent of the world's market. We are not holding our own, and the reason is

The government cannot shrug its shoulders and say that it is not its responsibility to sell wheat. The Prime Minister went to Winnipeg on June 2 and told the people of Canada that the government is going to sell 1,300 million bushels of wheat over the next three years. I thank the house for its indulgence and I am just about through, Mr. Speaker. I should like to close by making one other point.
The farmers have been assured by the Prime Minister that there is every prospect of being able to export an average of 430 million bushels of wheat a year for the next three years. The farmers have produced the wheat. A very large part of it is still on the farms. I have talked to farmers on the prairies who have 30,000, 40,000 or 50,000 bushels of grain on their farms. The farmers have no money. As a result the merchants are giving them credit. When the merchants cannot give the farmers further credit then both the merchants and the farmers are in trouble. The whole western economy is feeling the pinch of a serious situation.
I say to the government that our patience on this side of the house is exhausted. When the members of the government go across this country, and when the Prime Minister visits western Canada, they will find that the patience of the farmers is even more taxed than ours. Therefore I hope that instead of making the usual excuses and employing the usual stalling devices, the government will give the house some satisfactory reply today.
The members of this house would like to know from the Minister of Agriculture, first, what interim, short-term measures the government proposes to introduce at this time to put money into the pockets of the western farmers and to sustain the western economy. Second, we hope to hear a statement from the Minister of Industry, Trade

Alleged Failure to Aid Western Farmers and Commerce, or failing that from the acting minister, the hon. member for Saskatoon-Humboldt (Mr. Lang), on what long-term measures the government proposes in order to sell 1,300 million bushels of wheat over the next three years. If the government can give us satisfaction on those two points, I can assure the government that the farmers of this country will be most grateful. If the government has no answer, then the farmers of this country are going to be very angry indeed, as the government members will find out to their sorrow.

speechtext:
Surely the minister recognizes the need to help our farmers. Considering the number of times the minister has been embarrassed by having to stand up in the house and say that certain programs are under review and that others are being considered, he must surely have reached the point where he is prepared to do something effective for the farmers of his constituency and of the rest of Canada. He knows as well as anyone else how to bring about action.
At this stage of the session it is ridiculous for us to be pressing the government to help western farmers who face difficult cash positions and a serious crisis. The government's failure to show even the slightest interest in this situation makes the situation all the worse. Short-run prospects are gloomy and long-run prospects unnecessarily gloomy. Farmers are only human. If the Canadian government intends to drive them off the farm its present attitude of indifference will bring that about. Nothing could be better calculated to do that than the government's present attitude.
There is no indication, Mr. Speaker, that the government realizes or recognizes that Canadian wheat is one of this country's greatest material assets. There is no indication that the government intends to capitalize on modern Canadian wheat farms which are among the world's most efficient food producing units. The government, apparently is prepared to throw away one of the greatest advantages this country has in international trade. Other grains are important but the grains of major importance, of course, are wheat, oats and barley. And here, as the Canadian Federation of Agriculture so aptly put it, are the great issues of 1969. Here is where the government has shown nothing but failure.
Although the size of the world market in past years has increased, Canada has not shared in that expansion. Since 1963 our sales patterns have remained steady. The government has made no new efforts or incentives. On the international scene we face heavy competition, often from subsidized grains grown in other countries. On the domestic
June 17, 1969	COMMONS
scene we have a fantastic hold-over from the previous year which lies on the farms. The leader of the New Democratic party spoke most eloquently about this matter. Millions of bushels of grain remain stored on farms, many farmers not having delivered a bushel of wheat for months. This has meant for them months of waiting without a penny coming in and all the time our farmers' dollars going out to meet the ever-increasing cost brought about by high interest rates which the minister introduced a few months ago in this area.
Personal tragedy stalks many farmers on the western prairies today. Having been encouraged by this government, they invested heavily in capital equipment last year. They borrowed money and now the banks, equipment dealers and others are pressing for their money. Foreclosures of mortgages are threatened and equipment seizures are being discussed. Obviously the money supply is drying up in many small towns where continuing wheat deliveries to the elevators are essential to normal life. That essential ingredient has been denied to the western farmer because of the government's inaction. Because of the lack of cash and because of the credit squeeze, businesses which normally carry the western farmer over the thin spots are themselves pressed for cash. As a result they are pressing the farmers. Fuel dealers, food stores, utility companies and consumer credit firms are all now being forced to demand payment from farmers who lack cash and as a result are in desperate straits.
Not only has the federal government done nothing about getting some cash circulating again in the west but it has refused even to acknowledge that there is a problem. Are we to equate the just society with the callous society? It certainly looks that way. This government has gone beyond ignoring the problem; it has made it worse. Inflation, rising credit costs and continuing high taxes multiply the problem.
Surely I need not take up the time of the house in demonstrating the serious plight of the western farmer. Our long-term economic indicators show that our farmers must sell more wheat and undergo certain adjustments. We were reminded during the federal election campaign that the Prime Minister is good at selling wheat. On television I saw him saying not so long ago that in recent years we have not done too well in selling wheat and that we must improve our performance. He undertook to sell an average of 430 million bushels per year. Now he is apparently saying that it
Alleged Failure to Aid Western Farmers is not the government's job to sell wheat. I suggest that we ought to establish a new selling agency with a long-term policy regarding sales of wheat. I do not think the Canadian Wheat Board would be suitable. I understand that private marketing organizations in the United States have successfully marketed a good deal of wheat abroad. I believe the government ought to confront the government of the United States with facts. Our two countries ought to reach an understanding. After all, we have a common interest in marketing wheat and maintaining markets. In the long run nothing is to be gained by cutting prices because the demand for wheat is inelastic. We do not enlarge the market by reducing prices. Hence I say that the government has failed abysmally. It has failed to maintain our share of the market and to reach an understanding with the United States. Both countries must make certain that we have steady and orderly markets for our wheat.
While we talk about the size of the wheat hold-over and what that may mean to our future, I think we ought to see just how big the hold-over is in relation to our markets. I understand that in 1960 the world market for wheat was about one billion bushels. At that time there was a world surplus of about 2.5 billion bushels, of which about .7 billion bushels was in Canada. In other words, the world carryover in 1960 equalled two and a half times the annual world wheat market. At the end of the 1968 crop year I understand that the world wheat market had risen to about two billion bushels, and the carryover was about 1.5 billion bushels. Clearly, in 1968 wheat reserves were less than one year's annual sales. The wheat surplus will be bigger at the end of this crop year and a substantial percentage of that surplus will be held in Canada. Nevertheless I doubt that the carryover will exceed the requirements of world markets as a whole for one year.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
Of course I understand there has been a difference in the mix since then, and that a substantial part of the market is now in the form of lower quality grains. I do not believe our farmers have been encouraged to enter into the production of those grains. In any event, Mr. Speaker, it is important to relate carryovers to world demand and, if my information is correct, even with the large surplus that we have on hand in Canada it is only the equivalent of one year's world demand for wheat, compared with two and a half years'
10256	COMMONS
Alleged Failure to Aid Western Farmers world demand for wheat in 1960. This puts the matter in clear perspective.
We must remember that the production of wheat goes up and down. There is a succession of good years and a succession of dry years. Therefore I do not think we have any particular reason to be too pessimistic about the long-term view. At least I think we should relate our reserves to demand.
Of course if we regard wheat as a valuable resource which we pay elevator companies for storing, then possibly we should review the charges made by elevator companies for storage. Maybe we are paying relatively too much for storing and not enough for handling grain. Looking ahead, sir, if we regard wheat as a valuable asset, although we cannot sell it this year it may be that consideration should be given to some form of storage payment on the farms with a quota as to size, and of course payments would cease once the wheat was called for by the Wheat Board. This could certainly encourage the preservation of wheat which otherwise under present conditions may be allowed to go to rot.
If this asset is valuable there is no particular reason that the farmer on the farm should have to bear the whole cost of carrying it, whereas the elevator companies are paid for carrying it in their elevators. In addition, of course, over a period of time such a program would help the farmer with his cash position. However, it would not meet the contingency, the crisis, point out in the motion put forward by the Leader of the New Democratic party, which is the farmer's need for some substantial cash at the present time.
Reference was also made to the two-price system for wheat promised by the former Liberal prime minister. I am not making objections to this proposal, but I cannot help but recognize that it would add something to the load of the Canadian consumer at a time when he is being hard-pressed by higher prices and additional taxes imposed by the government, especially the vicious, regressive 2 per cent social development tax which bears particularly heavily on those who can least afford to pay it.

I am not objecting to the program. I am pointing out some of the limitations of it. If it were not made retroactive it would not provide the immediate cash that the farmer

needs now. I hope the minister will produce some long-range plans even if he is not able to produce any immediate assistance, which seems to be the case. It seems to me the government has worked itself into a position where it has left itself with only two options. Either it can stand by and let large numbers of farmers go down the drain, with economic difficulties piling up for western communities, for the economy of western Canada and indeed for Canada as a whole, or it can do something in the form of acreage payments. If the government had acted earlier it could have adopted a variety of programs to meet this emergency. If it believed it necessary for some of the wheat lands to be put into grass we could have adopted such a program earlier, but now such a program would be too late to help the farmers with their immediate problems. The government has boxed itself in to such an extent that an acreage payment is about the only way it can act now to provide the immediate assistance needed by the farmers. However, Mr. Speaker, I and my colleagues are prepared to support any reasonable plan which the government is prepared to put forward to meet this emergency.
During the election campaign the Prime Minister undertook not only to produce exports of 430 million bushels a year but also to give income assistance to farmers. Under the plan they would contribute to a fund in good years and draw income from it in bad years. I have not been in this house every minute since the session opened but I do not think I have heard the Prime Minister or the Minister of Agriculture make any pronouncement about when they will bring any such program into effect. I think that was about the greatest piece of hypocrisy I have heard for some time in election campaigns, and that is saying a good deal.
If the minister has the self-respect that I believe he has, or had, he would take rather drastic action to bring this matter forcefully to the government's attention. Certainly there is no legislation before the house for any program of income maintenance or assistance to farmers. As I say, in the circumstances the government will probably be driven to some form of acreage payment. Some such measure
June 17, 1969	COMMONS
is needed to try to tide the farmers over their immediate problems, to avoid the collapse of the farm industry and farm communities.
This afternoon we may hear a lot of talk about the fight against inflation. We are all engaged in the fight against inflation. It may be necessary to balance the budget. I appreciate the importance of a balanced budget in these conditions. I recognize the necessity of maintaining defences of some sort. But surely when one considers the dire difficulties of an important sector of the Canadian economy one is not necessarily going to try to preserve a balance in the budget, to maintain a state of surplus when that surplus is largely the result of inflation.
I am not suggesting that acreage payments are enough in themselves. A new crop is coming on. The elevators are plugged now. There may be some dispute about how much there will be to carry over, but it will be a great deal. The other day I heard the minister speak about the possibility of a drought. He said "drouth"; down east we say drought. We understand it means the same thing-no rain.
I got the impression the minister was rather hoping for that sort of thing. It may not have been intended and may have come from his subconscious.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall not abuse the hospitality of the house by taking much more time. I should like to emphasize that this is not just a western problem. We cannot divide this country into sectors and say it is all right because it only affects one part of the country and so on. We are all Canadians and it affects the whole Canadian economy. We can argue if we like that this is not an emergency situation, but there remains a crisis and the very least the government can do is give a very clear indication in this debate that it intends to act. I have very little
Alleged Failure to Aid Western Farmers hope this will take place, but I am an optimistic person by nature. The wheat farmers are in serious danger of losing their farms. Many of them are our best farmers who have experienced difficulty partly because they followed the course recommended by the government.
The second reason this matter is quite important, aside from all economic difficulties, is the refusal of the government to come to the aid of the farmers of western Canada in this time of crisis. This is contributing directly to the dangerous and growing sense of grievance in western Canada. Let us speak frankly. There is a growing feeling in western Canada that this is an eastern government which does not know and does not care about the problems of western Canada. This is the time to argue about the accuracy of this belief. I believe that the government time after time has been inexcusably insensitive in its approach to these problems. I believe it has shown more understanding of the Algerian problem-and the minister knows my concern about that. There could be serious consequences from this grievance. One is the hostility toward the languages bill which has become a symbol, to some extent, of the western grievances.
I have had some sympathy for the Minister of Agriculture. There are two attitudes he can take toward his job. One is to try to protect and help the Canadian farmer get action in respect of his agricultural problems. The other way, which he seems to have chosen to date, is to try to protect the government which he serves. That is what he has been doing. He has spent a year making excuses to western farmers and telling them all the reasons that the grain could not be dried, moved or sold. Seldom have we had a government of Canada that has directed more effort to explaining problems and less effort to resolving them.
I shall close as I started by saying to my hon. friend, the Minister of Agriculture, that if he does not have some definite word today, let him follow the course of the former Minister of Transport and then we will see a lot of action on the part of the government.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we undertake again today a discussion which is strangely similar to many others which we have held on various aspects of the economic activity of our country.
I listened carefully to the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) as well as
Alleged Failure to Aid Western Farmers to the leader of the New Democratic party (Mr. Douglas) who said that to solve the wheat problem in western Canada, the present Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) should resign. The resignation of the former Minister of Transport (Mr. Hellyer), who was responsible for housing in Canada, is given as an example on the ground that he did what was called for in the circumstances. But that did not solve the housing problem because it got even worse.
If the Minister of Agriculture were replaced by another in the same conditions, what would that change?
If the portfolio of the Minister of Agriculture were given to the Leader of the Opposition, what would happen? We would be stuck with the same old system. Indeed, the decision-making people are blamed rather than the system itself.
As for myself, I do not suggest that the Minister of Agriculture should resign, but rather that he put into practice what he preached during the many years when he was a Creditiste member.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-FAILURE TO RELIEVE ALLEGED CRITICAL CASH POSITION OF WESTERN CANADIAN FARMERS
speechtext: He knows what to do.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-FAILURE TO RELIEVE ALLEGED CRITICAL CASH POSITION OF WESTERN CANADIAN FARMERS
speechtext:
He certainly does.
Mr. Speaker, I remember the days when the Hon. Alvin Hamilton was minister of agriculture in the Conservative government, and the then member for Medicine Hat, the present Minister of Agriculture, told the minister of agriculture exactly the same things we are telling him today. That means the situation has not changed. Here, in the house, we sure look smart.
One day, we blame the government as this motion does, and I quote:
That this house condemns the government for its failure to take steps to relieve the critical cash position of farmers in Western Canada.
A "critical cash position", what does that mean? There may be some who do not understand that, but it means that western farmers are "broke", that they have no money. Yesterday, we had the bad "cash situation" of housing, the day before, that of the Ontario corn producers. We also have the bad "cash" situation of the Maritime provinces where the producers are stuck with a potato crop they cannot sell. Today, we have that of the western wheat producer. 
June 17, 1969
The leader of the New Democratic party said: That the economy of the western provinces is terribly depressed and it is true. But when we look at the whole of Canada, there is recession almost everywhere.
The province of Quebec is having problems with its dairy production, because the subsidies paid the milk producers have been lowered.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
The province of Quebec is the greatest producer of milk while Ontario is the greatest producer of corn. The situation is difficult for everyone and the farmers' income is going down. What is offered as a solution? Let us look at the inconsistency, at the folly of the government. And) as I said, we live in a world of crazy people and we are governed by the most remarkable among them.
For weeks relentless efforts are made tc come to an agreement in order to grant $50,000 loans so as to enable the farmers to survive, to buy machinery, to pay less interest.
There is no money left to help the farmers. They are allowed to get in debt and they are told to improve their means of production. Today there is an overproduction of wheat. No one knows what to do with it.
The Minister of Agriculture is quite right to walk along behind the curtains. He has no solution to offer and he is better there than sitting in his seat. He is unable to make a decision, to suggest an appropriate solution. What is the purpose of granting loans to farmers if our production cannot be disposed of? What is the use of loans to western farmers who are faced at this time with a wheat production for which they do not receive a red cent? To get them in debt? Farmers will not even be able to meet their obligations or pay off their loans. They are faced with a wheat surplus.
Part of last year's crop spent the winter under the snow in Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Alberta. Grain was threshed this spring and last year's grain has not been sold. This year, the farmers must borrow money from banks, credit unions and caisses populaires for seeding. There is even talk of paying the western farmers so much per acre not to produce wheat.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) tells us there is but one way of improving our standard of living, it is to increase productivity. How clever! Get into debt, borrow, and then increase your productivity, and after that, do

June 17, 1969	COMMONS
what you can with your products, we cannot help you to sell them.
Do you think the Minister of Agriculture spoke like that when he was sitting here with us?
It seems that when he left our side, he also left his intelligence behind. As for him, he lost everything and went to the other side of the House, with the Liberals. He speaks no longer the same language. Now that he is a Minister of Agriculture, it is as if he had lost all sense of values.
When the minister was Creditiste and used to go to the constituency of Medicine Hat, he did not talk as he does today; he used to say to the western farmers, to the farmers of Medicine Hat: "Believe me, I am familiar with agriculture and, being with the Liberals,
I will be in a position to do more for you than when I was a Creditiste." Look at him today; he is betraying the farmers of his constituency, of his province and of his country because he no longer dares to criticize the financial system. He used to know where the problem lay. Today, he no longer does. But he knows, for instance, that the problem is not a production problem. And that applies to all farm products, whether it be wheat in the West, potatoes in the Maritimes, milk in Quebec, or corn in Ontario and so on.
The minister suggests no answer. Compelling him to resign would be of no avail. What is the purpose of putting another cipher in his place if the same system remains unchanged?
Committees are set up. Recently, the members of the committee on Agriculture-I see the parliamentary secretary to the minister (Mr. Cote)-travelled across Canada to meet farmers at home. They realized there were wheat problems in the west, as the leader of the New Democratic party brilliantly explained earlier. They went to Ontario. They came to Quebec. They met farmers at the Chateau Frontenac, because that is where, apparently, the best land is to be found.
